cues.text: Bishop Through a Historic Transition
Sylvester I became bishop of Rome on January 31, 314, barely a year after the Edict of Milan had ended the great persecutions.
He remained pope for twenty-one years — one of the longest pontificates of the ancient Church — spanning virtually the entirety of Emperor Constantine 's reign.
During that time, Christianity moved from a persecuted minority faith to the favored religion of the empire.
Constantine's Great Churches
During Sylvester's pontificate, Constantine sponsored Rome's greatest Christian basilicas.
These included the basilica and baptistery of the Lateran , adjoining the former imperial palace that became the pope's own residence.
They also included the church of the Sessorian palace, known as Santa Croce, and the original basilica of St. Peter's over the Apostle's tomb on the Vatican Hill.
The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Sylvester, as bishop of the city, undoubtedly assisted in these vast building projects even if Constantine's imperial patronage funded them.
The Council of Nicaea
Sylvester did not personally travel to attend the momentous Council of Nicaea in 325, which condemned the Arian heresy and produced the Nicene Creed.
He was represented there by two legates.

Historians believe the crucial Greek term homoousios — 'of one substance,' the very word securing the Creed's affirmation of Christ's full divinity — was likely agreed upon with Sylvester's input before the council convened.
Legend and the Donation of Constantine
Centuries after his death, Sylvester became the central figure of an elaborate and entirely legendary tradition.
It claimed that he personally baptized Constantine in Rome, curing him of leprosy in the process.
Other evidence historically undermines this story: Constantine was in fact baptized near death by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.
This legend gave rise to the notorious medieval forgery known as the Donation of Constantine .
It purported to record vast privileges and territories the emperor granted to Sylvester and his papal successors.
Exposed as fraudulent only in the fifteenth century, it had nevertheless powerfully shaped medieval ideas of papal authority for many centuries.
Legacy
Sylvester I is remembered as one of the first popes to be venerated as a saint without having died a martyr, presiding as he did over a Church finally at peace rather than under persecution.
Though legendary embellishments later attached to his name obscure the historical reality of his pontificate, his genuine role overseeing Rome's transformation remains clear.
His quiet influence at Nicaea, together with that role in Christian building, marks him as a pivotal, if understated, figure in the Church's passage from the age of martyrs into the age of empire.
